awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: Semi-autonomous Image-guided Robotic Suturing System
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project will be a novel robotic technology for improving and automating vascular surgical procedures. A persistently high failure rate exists in microvascular surgery with anastomotic thromboses adversely affecting some of the most vulnerable populations.  The system aims to define a new paradigm by creating a novel system leveraging state-of-the-art imaging, machine learning, and advanced robotics to exceed the capabilities of human performance. The system aims to semi automate these procedures to improve the rates of microvascular anastomotic success, reducing hospital lengths of stay, decreasing re-operations, diminish pain and suffering, and improve longevity of at-risk populations. The technology presents a novel technological platform for the $6 billion market robotic surgery growing at 15% each year. 

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project will design and develop a novel robotic surgery system reducing the rates of anastomotic thrombosis in microsurgery. The first objective is to develop a novel optical coherence tomography imaging system integrated with a robotic microvascular suturing tool for microvascular surgery. The second objective will be to test the accuracy of an optical coherence tomography imaging for needle placement in microvascular anastomosis, using synthetic and explanted biologic blood vessels of the images. Optical coherence tomography images will be compared to electron micrographs for detection of vascular intima, media, and adventitia. The third objective will be to develop machine learning algorithms for accurate image interpretation to guide needle placement using a series of experimental acquired data to achieve the level of control precision needed for micro-anastomosis. The end result of this project will be to demonstrate technical feasibility for the prototype system.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Project Outcomes Report NSF SBIR Award 2423546

Surgical Vision Systems, Inc. 

300 West Pratt St, Ste 200

Baltimore MD 21201

https://surgicalvisionsystems.com/

Surgeons who connect blood vessels as small as one millimeter in diameter— in cancer and breast reconstruction, bypass surgery, and limb salvage — face a 10–15% rate of clot formation at the connection (anastomosis) despite technical advances and modern post-surgical care. The complication of anastomotic failure can cost a patient a flap, a limb, or a return trip to the operating room. Surgical Vision Systems, Inc. (SVS) undertook this NSF SBIR Phase I project to determine whether a robotic system could place stitches in small blood vessels more precisely and more consistently than the human hand, building on the µ-STAR robotic suturing platform developed in the Krieger Lab at Johns Hopkins University. SVS pursued two goals: an imaging system with resolution adequate to visualize sections of the boundary of a 1 mm vessel in real time; and a mechanism able to place sutures at the spacing required for leak proof closure.

Both goals were met. The team built and demonstrated an imaging system that resolves features of a 1 mm vessel to better than 1/10 of a millimeter, enough detail to guide where the suture needle enters the vessel wall and how deeply it passes through it. To achieve this, the team integrated an off-the-shelf 1 × 1 millimeter fiber-optic camera with a custom gimbal system that identifies the vessel’s center and calculates the precise bite depth based on the vessel’s diameter. The team also designed and tested a suture placement mechanism that positions the needle in increments of roughly 1/6 of a millimeter, allowing 6 evenly spaced stitches to be placed around the circumference of a 1 mm vessel — the pattern surgeons use by hand today. This precision is enabled by a high-resolution motorized holder that accurately rotates the vessel, working in tandem with a bespoke suture guidance system. The entire system was validated through a progression of 3D-printed models, synthetic tissues, and explanted swine blood vessels. The complete suturing prototype occupies less than one cubic foot, small enough to be a modular addition to an existing operating table rather than requiring a dedicated console. Further size reductions along with enhanced imaging and suturing resolutions are feasible.

Together, these results show that image-guided robotic suturing at the microvascular scale is technically achievable. If carried forward, the approach could make this demanding operation more reliable and more widely available, including at hospitals without a fellowship-trained microvascular surgeon on staff, benefiting patients with advanced cancer, diabetes, and severe vascular disease. In the next phase, the company will advance the microvascular suturing system through animal testing and into eventual clinical use.
